strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: UniMER-1M (1.06M samples) is 6-10× larger than prior MER datasets with balanced length distribution and diverse expression types (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE), addressing important gaps in real-world MER benchmarking

Comprehensive evaluation methodology: Four-way test categorization (simple/complex printed, screen-captured, handwritten) provides nuanced assessment and clearly reveals existing methods' failures on complex/noisy expressions

Strong and consistent empirical results: Outperforms SOTA across all test categories with significant improvements on complex expressions (+0.226 BLEU over Pix2tex on CPE) and competitive results on handwritten benchmarks
Systematic ablation studies: Tables 2-4 effectively isolate contributions of dataset diversity, data augmentation, and LAM components
Practical value: Addresses important real-world MER challenges (length variation, noise, domain diversity) with working system and dataset release
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Core contribution is standard Swin Transformer + mBART encoder-decoder; Length-Aware Module (LAM) is relatively simple (attention + pooling + MLP), with marginal empirical benefit (Table 4: ~2% BLEU on CPE, <1% on most other sets), raising questions about necessity and complexity-benefit tradeoff

Unfair comparison with prior methods: Comparing UniMERNet (trained on 1.06M samples) against Pix2tex (158K) and Texify (30K) conflates dataset scale with architectural improvements; critical missing ablation is retraining Pix2tex/Texify on UniMER-1M to isolate model contributions from data scale effects

Insufficient dataset novelty: SPE/CPE are purely synthetic (rendered LaTeX); SCE contains only ~4,744 unique samples from PDFs; HWE is straightforward combination of existing CROHME + HME100K datasets; missing details on data balancing strategy, inter-annotator agreement, and automatic annotation error rates

Incomplete experimental analysis: No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; missing computational cost analysis (inference speed, model size, memory); lacks error analysis, failure mode characterization, and explanation of when/why LAM helps; ExpRate metric inconsistently reported

Orthogonal augmentation benefits: Image augmentation improvements (Table 3) are independent of architectural design and could benefit any baseline model, making it difficult to isolate UniMERNet's specific contributions

Limited scope of 'real-world': Only evaluates LaTeX output; SCE sampling from 1,000 PDFs may not fully represent document diversity; no end-to-end document understanding evaluation; claims of 'universal' and 'unprecedented' are somewhat overstated

Methodological details underspecified: 'Length' definition unclear (tokens vs. characters); SmoothL1 loss choice for length prediction not justified; loss weight selection (λ₁=1, λ₂=0.5) arbitrary without ablation; LAM architectural modifications to mBART not precisely detailed
Minimal qualitative analysis: Figure 5 shows only 3 examples; no systematic error analysis or discussion of limitations; insufficient examination of when and why the proposed method fails

strengths: Large-scale, diverse dataset (UniMER-1M with 1M training samples) addressing multiple expression types (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE) with comprehensive multi-dimensional test set (UniMER-Test)
Solid empirical results with substantial improvements over SOTA baselines on complex scenarios (22.6% BLEU improvement over Pix2tex on CPE; 19.6% on SCE)
Well-motivated practical problem with clear demonstration of existing method failures on real-world noisy/complex expressions (Figure 1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablation studies, cross-dataset comparisons (CROHME, HME100K), and multiple metrics (BLEU, EditDistance, ExpRate)
Thorough documentation of dataset construction pipeline with clear categorization of expression types and multi-source data collection procedures
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core architecture is standard transformer encoder-decoder (Swin + mBART); Length-Aware Module contribution is minimal and shows marginal empirical gains (Table 4: +2% on CPE, negligible on other subsets), with unclear theoretical justification for why predicting length via visual features is superior to implicit decoder learning

Overstated dataset novelty: SPE/CPE (~835K) are synthetically rendered LaTeX (not true real-world diversity); SCE is based on only 1,000 PDFs with manual annotation by 2 annotators with no inter-annotator agreement reported; HWE is simply aggregation of existing datasets (CROHME + HME100K), not novel contribution

Experimental methodology flaws: Table 2 ablation conflates data scale and diversity (UniMER-1M vs. Pix2tex+HWE comparison doesn't control for total data size); missing validation set and hyperparameter selection procedure; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported

Reproducibility concerns: dataset/model availability URL missing/blank despite claim in abstract; augmentation strategy incompletely specified; hyperparameter choices (λ₁=1, λ₂=0.5) lack justification; no validation procedure documented

Insufficient analysis and weak justification of core contributions: no failure analysis or error categorization despite 8%+ error rate on HWE; LAM motivation lacks theoretical grounding or deeper empirical analysis; minimal ablation of which augmentations are necessary; missing cross-dataset generalization study beyond comparison tables

Overclaimed 'universality': despite title, 33% BLEU drop from SPE (0.917) to SCE (0.616) demonstrates non-universal performance; SCE subset (4,774 training samples, 20% of test set) lacks depth for robust real-world generalization claims

Unfair baseline comparisons: Pix2tex/Texify not designed for all four expression types; Nougat comparison requires test image modification (adding random text), undermining fair evaluation; LVLMs dismissed as 'mediocre' without rigorous head-to-head testing

strengths: Large-scale dataset contribution: UniMER-1M with 1.06M samples substantially exceeds prior datasets (previously 158K), addressing data scarcity in MER
Comprehensive multi-dimensional evaluation: UniMER-Test covers four real-world scenarios (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE) with 23,789 samples, going beyond narrow prior benchmarks
Well-motivated problem: Clearly demonstrates gap where SOTA methods achieve ~90% BLEU on simple expressions but drop to 1-34% on complex/noisy scenarios (Figure 1)
Strong empirical results: BLEU improvements of 0.226 (CPE) and 0.196 (SCE) over Pix2tex/Texify; competitive on handwritten benchmarks (+1.5-5.3% ExpRate on CROHME)
Thorough ablation studies: Tables 2-4 systematically validate dataset diversity, augmentation benefits, and LAM contributions across subsets
Transparent methodology: Detailed descriptions of data collection procedures (rendering, annotation, aggregation) enhance reproducibility
Practical relevance: Addresses genuine challenges in document analysis with applications to scientific document extraction
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Standard encoder-decoder architecture (Swin Transformer + mBART), conventional augmentation techniques, and straightforward length prediction module—primarily engineering/data-centric rather than methodological innovation
Modest LAM contribution: Table 4 shows only 2.3% improvement on CPE; negligible gains on other subsets. Ablation suggests UniMER-1M dataset and augmentation are primary performance drivers, not LAM

Insufficient LAM analysis: No ablation of loss weight λ₂, no visualization of length predictions vs. ground truth, no explanation of why LAM helps only CPE, missing comparison with prior HME length-prediction work

Data source concerns: SPE/CPE are synthetic (distribution shift from test); SCE derived from only 1,000 PDFs yielding 4,744 unique expressions; SCE quality relies on Mathpix OCR without inter-annotator agreement reporting; HWE is mere aggregation of existing datasets

Incomplete technical specification: Vague LAM integration into mBART (Section 4.1), missing architecture details (attention heads, hidden dimensions), no justification for 1024 max length or handling of longer expressions, no ablation of loss weights (λ₁=1, λ₂=0.5)

Evaluation limitations: BLEU score insensitivity to structural correctness, character-level edit distance insufficient for semantic errors, unfair comparison with Nougat (modified inputs), no statistical significance testing, Figure 5 provides only 3 qualitative examples
Missing failure analysis: No discussion of failure modes, error categorization, or systematic weaknesses; unclear when/why model struggles; no analysis of extremely long expressions (max length 7037)

Generalization concerns: No cross-dataset evaluation (UniMER-1M→CROHME transfer), no domain-specific analysis (physics/chemistry/CS formulas), no consideration of non-LaTeX markup formats, limited language-specific insights despite Chinese/English mix
Unexplained phenomena: Table 3 shows augmentation effectiveness decreases with stronger base model (2.5% on Pix2tex vs 0.57% on UniMER-1M for SCE)—counter-intuitive result not discussed

Reproducibility gaps: Vague augmentation specifications (libraries, probabilities), no per-augmentation ablation, no wall-clock training time, dataset/code access promised but not available in submission
Incomplete comparison: No head-to-head comparison with recent vision-language models beyond limited Nougat testing; insufficient analysis of why Pix2tex/Texify underperform

Presentation issues: Dense Figure 4, unclear notation (Eq. 2, index c), misleading 'Length-Aware' terminology (predicts rather than adapts to length), somewhat marketing-oriented claims ('unprecedented', 'universal')

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: UniMER-1M (1.06M samples) represents a significant advance in scale and diversity over prior MER datasets (100k-200k), with thoughtful coverage of multiple formula types (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE) and real-world scenarios

Comprehensive evaluation benchmark: UniMER-Test with 23,789 diverse samples addresses documented gaps in existing benchmarks, particularly for complex, noisy, and handwritten expressions, establishing a valuable new evaluation standard

Thorough experimental validation: Extensive ablation studies, depth configuration analysis, augmentation impact assessment, and pre-training analysis provide solid empirical support with multiple metrics (BLEU, EditDistance, ExpRate)

Well-motivated architecture: The three identified challenges (visual similarity, spatial information, inference speed) are clearly articulated and the proposed solutions (FGE, CE, RSW, SA) follow logically from these constraints

Reproducibility focus: Detailed implementation specifications (hyperparameters, rendering settings, augmentation procedures, XeLaTeX configuration) and commitment to release code/data support reproducibility
Practical efficiency gains: Achieves ~23% speed improvement (5.06 vs. 4.12 FPS) while maintaining or improving accuracy, valuable for real-world deployment
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Individual components (FGE: modified patch embedding; CE: standard depthwise convolution; SA: ResNet's squeeze-excitation) are established techniques. The paper presents engineering optimization rather than algorithmic innovation

Data-model attribution ambiguity: Table 5 reveals that when Texify is trained on UniMER-1M, residual improvements over UniMERNet are modest (SPE: +0.009, CPE: +0.025, SCE: +0.027 BLEU). Most performance gains stem from the dataset rather than architectural contributions

Data contamination risk not adequately addressed: 89% of UniMER-1M LaTeX comes from ArXiv; Table 6 shows 16M additional image-text pairs from ArXiv used for pre-training. The paper does not credibly rule out formula overlap between training/pre-training and test sets, and SPE explicitly reuses Pix2tex's test set

Insufficient statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or bootstrap analysis. Performance differences of 1-2% on smaller subsets (HWE: 6,332 samples) lack statistical justification. No inter-annotator agreement reported for manual SCE annotation

Incomplete real-world performance analysis: Despite the title's claim of 'real-world' capability, absolute performance on realistic data remains limited (SCE: 0.626 BLEU; HWE improvement +0.007 BLEU vs. Texify*). HWE gains minimal benefit from ArXiv-heavy pre-training, yet this limitation is underexplored

Pre-training data inaccessibility and underspecification: The 16M image-text pairs are described as 'in-house' and unavailable, compromising reproducibility. The procedure for creating pre-training data lacks documentation, making results difficult for others to verify or extend

Overstated claims about universality: Title and framing claim 'universal' and 'real-world' capabilities, but performance gaps on authentic data (SCE, HWE) and small absolute gains on handwritten expressions contradict these claims

Absence of systematic error analysis: Only 3 cherry-picked qualitative examples in Figure 5. No investigation of failure modes, performance by formula complexity/length, or systematic categorization of errors

Missing reproduction details: LaTeX normalization rules stated as 'adjusted' but not formally specified; Squeeze Attention's dimensionality reduction factor not quantified; perceptual hashing threshold for SCE deduplication not provided

strengths: Large-scale dataset contribution: UniMER-1M (1.06M samples) substantially exceeds existing MER datasets and provides unprecedented scale for model training
Comprehensive evaluation benchmark: UniMER-Test covers diverse real-world scenarios (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE) with thoughtful inclusion of screen-captured and handwritten expressions
Thorough experimental methodology: Extensive ablation studies clearly demonstrate individual component contributions; multiple model variants (T/S/B) and pre-training analysis provided
Practical speed-accuracy improvements: Achieves both accuracy gains (2-23% on CPE/SCE) and 21.6% speed improvement over Texify baseline
Implementation reproducibility: Detailed dataset construction methodology in appendix covering rendering, normalization, and augmentation strategies with clear pipeline descriptions
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Proposed modifications (FGE, CE, RSW, SA) are straightforward engineering optimizations rather than principled innovations; each component contributes ≤2% improvement individually, suggesting incremental rather than transformative advances

Confounded experimental comparison: Critical evidence shows Texify* (same architecture, UniMER-1M data) achieves 0.900 CPE/0.599 SCE vs. original Texify's 0.690/0.420, revealing most gains come from dataset/augmentation not architecture; unfair baseline comparison obscures true contribution breakdown

Limited dataset novelty: UniMER-1M reuses existing sources (Pix2tex 158K, CROHME 8.8K, HME100K 74.5K) with straightforward ArXiv-sourced rendering; no novel annotation methodology, uses standard XeLaTeX rendering identical to prior work

Missing experimental controls: No cross-dataset evaluation on prior benchmarks (IM2LATEX-100K, CROHME, HME100K); unclear pre-training impact; augmentation contribution not isolated; design choices (kernel size, stride, depth) lack justification

Small and potentially biased test set: SCE subset contains only 4,744 unique samples from 1,000 PDFs with questionable methodology (Mathpix circular dependency); no inter-annotator agreement reported; restricting evaluation to UniMER-Test prevents generalization assessment

Overclaimed contributions: Terms like 'universal' and 'first real-world MER study' are not well-justified; prior work (Pix2tex, Texify, Nougat) already addresses diverse scenarios; paper conflates dataset contribution with architectural innovation without clear delineation

strengths: Large-scale, well-curated dataset (1.06M samples) addressing real gap in MER research with thoughtful coverage of four distinct real-world scenarios (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE)
Comprehensive empirical validation including extensive ablations (Tables 2, 3, 7-9) systematically justifying each architectural component
Consistent improvements across all four evaluation subsets simultaneously while achieving both accuracy gains and 21.6% speed improvement over SOTA
Well-motivated technical contributions addressing specific MER challenges: FGE tackles fragmentation, ConvEnhance provides local-global balance, Squeeze Attention targets decoder bottleneck
Thoughtful dataset construction methodology including image-based deduplication for SCE using perceptual hashing and principled sampling to balance formula lengths and complexity
Practical value with multiple model variants (T, S, B) enabling speed-accuracy tradeoffs and promised code/data release supporting reproducibility
Detailed documentation of data collection, normalization procedures, and comprehensive statistical analysis of dataset properties
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: FGE is straightforward 3×3 convolution substitution, ConvEnhance is standard depthwise convolution, and Squeeze Attention lacks clear technical specification (reduction ratios, mechanism details remain vague)
Small test set sizes for real-world evaluation: SCE contains only 4,744 unique samples after deduplication; per-category test set sizes not clearly reported

Unfair experimental comparison: 16M in-house Arxiv pre-training data advantage not available to baselines; Table 6 shows even with same pre-training Texify* still underperforms, making it unclear if gains come from architecture or pre-training scale

Potential dataset bias toward synthetic expressions: massive CPE improvement (0.235) vs. modest SCE/HWE gains (0.206, 0.554) contradicts real-world robustness claims; SPE improvement only 0.009 suggests limited gains on simpler cases

Incomplete technical analysis: why removing Shift Window benefits the model receives insufficient justification; limited ablation on pre-training data amount; no computational cost analysis of added modules
HWE data entirely from existing datasets (CROHME, HME100K), not newly collected; SCE ground truth from Mathpix→manual correction without inter-annotator agreement reported
Evaluation metrics not optimal for formula recognition: BLEU borrowed from machine translation; character-level Edit Distance doesn't capture structural errors; ExpRate only applied to HWE
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing; FPS measured only at batch size 128; limited comparison across inference conditions
Insufficient error analysis: no categorization of failure modes, qualitative examples appear cherry-picked, missing investigation of formula-type-specific performance
Overclaimed contributions: description of Nougat comparison acknowledges unfairness (Nougat designed for full documents, test adapted with surrounding text) yet still claims advantage
